config.notificationPollingEnabled.title: Notifications: Poll for Unread Notifications
config.notificationPollingEnabled.descri: Periodically poll Forgejo instances for unread notifications and show VS Code alerts.
config.notificationPollingInterval.title: Notifications: Polling Interval
config.notificationPollingInterval.descr: Interval in seconds between notification polls. A value between 60 and 3600, defaulting to 300; one outside that range is refused.
config.useMockApi.title: Developer: Use Mock API
config.useMockApi.description: Use mock Forgejo API responses for offline development. Development use only; stripped from production builds, and read once at activation so a change needs a window reload.
config.mcpEnabled.title: MCP Server: Expose Instances to Agents
config.mcpEnabled.description: Expose the configured Forgejo instances to agent mode as MCP servers: 30 read-only tools by default, plus three write tools that are off by default and each behind its own setting. Turning this off withdraws the server definitions immediately and stops the workspace-repository mapping and the local broker; a client that is already connected keeps the server process it spawned until the window is reloaded.
MCP Write Tools: Create Issue Comment

Let AI agents create issue and pull request comments on your instances through the MCP tool `create_issue_comment`. Off by default. While it is on, an agent can leave public comments under your account: VS Code asks you to confirm each call, but you can turn that confirmation off for the tool, and a client other than VS Code may not implement it at all. Turn this on only when you intend to let the agent write, and read every comment it proposes before approving it.
config.mcpWriteTools.submitPullReview.ti: MCP Write Tools: Submit Pull Review
config.mcpWriteTools.submitPullReview.de: Let AI agents submit pending pull request reviews on your instances through the MCP tool `submit_pull_review`, with the verdict COMMENT, APPROVED or REQUEST_CHANGES. Off by default and separate from the comment switch: approving a pull request can satisfy branch protection, so this is the more consequential of the two. While it is on, an agent can leave public reviews and formal approvals under your account: VS Code asks you to confirm each call, but you can turn that confirmation off for the tool, and a client other than VS Code may not implement it at all. Turn this on only when you intend to let the agent review, and read every verdict it proposes before approving it.
config.mcpWriteTools.cancelActionRun.tit: MCP Write Tools: Cancel Action Run
config.mcpWriteTools.cancelActionRun.des: Let AI agents cancel pending or running Actions workflow runs on your instances through the MCP tool `cancel_action_run`. Off by default and separate from the comment and review switches. This one does not append text — it stops work that is already running, cancelling the run's pending or running jobs; the run has to be triggered again afterwards, which this tool does not do. While it is on, an agent can stop a running deployment, release job or test run under your account: VS Code asks you to confirm each call, but you can turn that confirmation off for the tool, and a client other than VS Code may not implement it at all. Turn this on only when you intend to let the agent stop runs, and check which run it names before approving it.
config.mcpWriteAuditToFile.title: MCP Write Tools: Audit to File
config.mcpWriteAuditToFile.description: Also append the MCP write-tool audit records to `mcp-write-audit.jsonl` in the extension's log folder (VS Code: "Developer: Open Logs Folder"), on top of the Forgejo Toolkit Output Channel. Each record is one JSON line with the caller, instance, repository, target, tool, dry-run flag, body size and digest, result and duration — never the comment text. The file is capped at 1 MB with two rolled files. Off by default: the audit stays in the Output Channel, where it is lost when the window closes.
config.multiWindowLease.title: Notifications: One Polling Window
config.multiWindowLease.description: Poll Forgejo instances and raise notification alerts from only one VS Code window at a time instead of every open window. The mode tries to hand that job to whichever window you are working in; if VS Code's focus state cannot be trusted on your platform, the current holder keeps the lease and the alerts stay with the lease-holding window, and no alert is lost. The other windows stay quiet but still load notifications when you open the view. Turn this off to let every window poll and alert on its own, which uses more requests but is the behaviour before this setting existed.
config.aiEnabled.title: AI: Enabled
config.aiEnabled.description: The whole AI area's own switch. On by default; while it is off no AI feature runs and no model is asked for anything — neither the chat models this editor offers nor an endpoint configured in `forgejoToolkit.aiProviders` — and nothing is sent anywhere for an AI feature. It is the layer above the per-feature switches: this one says "do not use AI at all", a feature's own switch (`forgejoToolkit.aiPreReview`, `forgejoToolkit.prDescription`) says "this feature is on", and the consent question a feature asks before it sends anything is what decides whether content leaves the machine and how much. Configuring endpoints, choosing a transport or a model, and setting a prompt scope all stay possible while it is off, so turning it back on needs no reconfiguration.
config.aiPreReview.title: AI Pre-Review
config.aiPreReview.description: Add an "AI Pre-Review Pull Request" action to the pull request diff editor: a chat model reads the pull request and proposes line-level review comments, you pick the ones you agree with one by one, and only those are written as drafts of a pending review. The extension never submits a review — the existing "Submit review" button stays the only way anything becomes public — and an unconfirmed comment writes nothing. Off by default; while it is off the command refuses and no content is sent anywhere. Turning it on sends the pull request's title, its base and head branch names, the changed-file paths with their additions/deletions and status, and the metadata (path, line, author, review state) of existing review comments to the chat model provider you configured in VS Code. What else may be sent — no code at all, the changed lines, the whole diff, or the changed files' own text — is decided by `forgejoToolkit.aiPreReviewPromptScope`, whose default `ask` means: the first pre-review shows one modal naming the provider and what each answer sends, nothing is requested or sent before you answer, and your answer is stored there.
config.aiPreReviewPromptScope.title: AI Pre-Review: Prompt Scope
config.aiPreReviewPromptScope.descriptio: What the prompt may carry during an AI pre-review. This is the only place the egress decision is made and the only place it is recorded: `ask` (the default) means you have not chosen yet, the next pre-review shows one modal naming the provider that would receive the content and what each answer sends, and your answer is written here — so the question is asked once, not once per run. The four stated scopes are `metadata-only` (the model sees no code at all), `changed-lines-only` (the added and removed lines, with the file and hunk headers that keep line numbers unambiguous), `full-diff` (the whole diff, including the unchanged context lines, without the files' own text) and `changed-files` (the whole diff plus the full text of every changed file at the pull request's head version — the most content, and the only scope under which the model can read the code around a change). Every scope is bounded: the changed-file table, the diff and the file texts are cut from the end when they exceed the shared budgets and the file count cap, and every cut is stated in the prompt itself. Only files the pull request changed are ever read or sent — no other file in the repository, no access token, no URL or host name, and never the body of an existing review comment.
config.aiPreReviewPromptScope.enumDescri: Ask before the next pre-review sends anything: one modal names the provider and what each answer would send, nothing is requested, sent or written until you answer, and your answer is stored in this setting.

Send no code at all — only the pull request's title and branch names, the changed-file paths with their line counts, and the metadata (path, line, author, review state) of existing review comments. The model cannot read a single changed line and can only comment on file-level matters.

Send the changed lines of code only — the added and removed lines of each file with its file and hunk headers, and none of the unchanged context lines around them. The cheapest scope under which the model still reads code.
Send the whole diff — every hunk of every changed file, including the unchanged context lines — but not the changed files' own text.

Send the whole diff and the full text of every changed file at the pull request's head version. The most content of any scope, and the only one under which the model reads the code around a change (error handling outside the hunk, callers and conventions elsewhere in the file); the file texts are cut from the end when the shared budget or the file cap is reached.
config.aiPreReviewModel.title: AI Pre-Review: Chat Model
config.aiPreReviewModel.description: Which chat model reviews a pull request, as `vendor/family` or `vendor/id` (an optional `@version` suffix is accepted too) — for example `deepseek/deepseek-flash`, or `copilot/gpt-4o` for the model a provider lists as id `gpt-4o` under vendor `copilot`. Case and surrounding spaces are ignored, and the name is matched against the models VS Code offers, so the first part must be the provider's vendor id and the second its family or model id, as the chat model picker shows them. Leave it empty — the default — and the next pre-review asks which model to use, then writes your answer here; fill it in and every run uses that one model without asking. The extension never picks a model for you and never switches between models: the command "AI Pre-Review: Choose Chat Model" changes this value later. A value that is not one of those forms, or that names a model VS Code does not offer, does not start the run — the message names what you configured and lists the models that are offered, each with its vendor/family and its input token budget — and a model whose input budget cannot hold the feature's instructions is refused too, never silently replaced by another one. The setting matters for privacy, not only for quality: the brief goes to the provider behind the model you name here.
config.prDescription.title: AI: Generate Pull Request Description
config.prDescription.description: Add a "Generate description" control to the create-pull-request form and to an existing pull request's edit dialog: a chat model drafts a description from the comparison the form holds — the commits between the two branches, with their subjects, bodies, authors and dates, and the path and status of every changed file — and fills it into the description field as an **editable** draft. You still create or save the pull request yourself; the extension never opens, fills in or submits it for you, and a draft it could not produce leaves the field exactly as you wrote it. Off by default; while it is off the control is hidden and nothing is read or sent. What else may be sent — the pull request's own diff (its hunks), the changed files' own text at the head branch, or no file content at all — is decided by `forgejoToolkit.prDescriptionPromptScope`, whose default `ask` means: the next draft shows one modal naming the provider and what each answer sends, nothing is requested or sent before you answer, and your answer is stored there. The scope `commits-and-diff` reads the pull request's own diff, so it is offered in an existing pull request's edit dialog and not on the create form, whose pull request does not exist yet.
config.prDescriptionPromptScope.title: AI: PR Description Prompt Scope
config.prDescriptionPromptScope.descript: What the prompt may carry when a pull request description is drafted. This is the only place that egress decision is made and the only place it is recorded: `ask` (the default) means you have not chosen yet, the next draft shows one modal naming the provider that would receive the content and what each answer sends, and your answer is written here — so the question is asked once, not once per draft. The three stated scopes are `commits-only` (the branch names, the commits with their subjects, bodies, authors and dates, and the path and status of every changed file — no file content), `commits-and-diff` (the same plus the pull request's own diff: the added and removed lines of every changed file with its file and hunk headers, exactly as the server reports the diff, and a binary file's change carries no hunks) and `commits-and-files` (the commits and the changed-file list plus the full text of the changed files at the head branch, the most content, and the only scope under which the model can read the code around a change). All of them are bounded: the commit list, the changed-file table, the diff and the file texts are cut from the end when they exceed the shared budgets and caps, and every cut is stated in the prompt itself. No access token and no URL or host name is ever sent. `commits-and-diff` needs a pull request that already exists, because it reads that pull request's own diff; the create form does not offer it, and a run configured with it there refuses by name instead of drafting from something else.
config.prDescriptionPromptScope.enumDesc: Ask before the next description sends anything: one modal names the provider and what each answer would send, nothing is requested, sent or written until you answer, and your answer is stored in this setting.

Send the branch names, the commits between them (subjects, bodies, authors and dates) and the path and status of every changed file. No file content leaves the machine, so the model can describe what the commits say changed but cannot read the code.

Send the commits and the changed-file list plus the pull request's own diff: the added and removed lines of every changed file with its file and hunk headers, exactly as the server reports the diff, so the model reads what actually changed rather than only what the commit messages say. A binary file's change arrives without hunks and is sent as the server reports it; no changed file's full text is sent, and no access token, URL or host name is ever sent. This answer reads the pull request's own diff, so it needs a pull request that already exists and is offered in an existing pull request's edit dialog.

Send the commits and the changed-file list, plus the full text of the changed files at the head branch. The most content, and the only scope under which the model can read the code around a change; the file texts are cut from the end when the shared budget or the file cap is reached.
config.issueTriage.title: AI: Issue Label Suggestions
config.issueTriage.description: Add a "Suggest labels" action to an issue's page: a chat model reads that issue's title and body and the repository's own label list, and proposes which labels apply. The extension writes **nothing**: the suggestions are shown one by one for you to tick, and applying them opens the issue's existing edit form, pre-filled with what you ticked, which you save yourself — no label is ever applied without that save, and the assignee field is not touched at all. Off by default; while it is off the action is not shown and nothing is read or sent. What else may be sent — the discussion comments, or none — is decided by `forgejoToolkit.issueTriagePromptScope`, whose default `ask` means: the next run shows one modal naming the provider and what each answer sends, nothing is requested or sent before you answer, and your answer is stored there. A suggestion that does not resolve to a label the same run read from the repository is dropped and counted rather than matched approximately. A repository that declares no label at all does not show the action, and the run refuses in its own words if a stale view asks anyway. The model comes from the same place the other AI features take theirs: your editor's models, chosen in a picker at the moment you ask because this feature keeps no model of its own, or a configured endpoint bound to `issueTriage`. A failure is reported and never retried on another model or the other transport, and with no usable model at all the action sends nothing and points at the Settings page.
config.issueTriagePromptScope.title: AI: Issue Label Suggestions Prompt Scope
config.issueTriagePromptScope.descriptio: What the prompt may carry when issue label suggestions are drafted. This is the only place that egress decision is made and the only place it is recorded: `ask` (the default) means you have not chosen yet, the next run shows one modal naming the provider that would receive the content and what each answer sends, and your answer is written here — so the question is asked once, not once per issue. The two stated scopes are `issue-only` (the issue's title and body, and the repository's label list — each label's name and description, with archived labels left out — so the model can pick from what this repository actually offers) and `issue-and-comments` (the same plus the discussion comments, each with its author and date). Both are bounded: the body, the label list and the comment list are cut from the end when they exceed the shared budgets, the comment count is capped, and every cut is stated in the prompt itself. Only one scope's content is ever sent — never the label list and the discussion by accident — and no access token, URL or host name is ever sent.
config.issueTriagePromptScope.enumDescri: Ask before the next triage run sends anything: one modal names the provider and what each answer would send, nothing is requested, sent or written until you answer, and your answer is stored in this setting.

Send the issue's own text — its title and body — plus the repository's label list (each label's name and description, archived labels excluded). No discussion comment leaves the machine, so the model triages from the issue as written and cannot read what has already been said about it.

Send everything `issue-only` sends plus the discussion: the comments with their authors and dates. The most content, and the only scope under which the model can take what has already been said into account; the comment list is capped and cut from the end when the shared budget is reached.
config.aiProviders.title: AI: Configured Endpoints
config.aiProviders.description: The OpenAI-compatible endpoints this extension may send to, as a list of objects. Each entry needs an `id` (letters, digits, `_`, `-`), a display `name`, and a `baseUrl` used exactly as written apart from a trailing slash — `/v1` is deliberately not appended, because an Azure URL and a gateway's `/openai/v1` would both be made wrong by it. Optional fields: `models` (the models this endpoint has, as `{ id, name }` — a declaration used to fill in the model picker, not a whitelist, so an empty list is allowed), `auth` (`bearer`, `api-key-header` for Azure's `api-key`, or `none` for a server that wants no credential), and `headers` (extra header names, including `api-version`, which is sent as a query parameter). Every `baseUrl` must be an absolute `http:` or `https:` URL without credentials in it: a `file:` or `data:` URL and a URL like `https://user:token@host` are refused, and a plain `http://` address is allowed but reported as unencrypted whenever a request goes to it. The API key and every custom header value are deliberately **not** here — they are stored in the editor's secret storage (keys `forgejoToolkit.aiProviderKey.<id>` and `forgejoToolkit.aiProviderHeader.<id>.<headerName>`), and a value written into this setting by hand is ignored rather than sent. Configuring an endpoint here sends nothing by itself: a feature must be bound to it and must be allowed to send, which is what `forgejoToolkit.aiEnabled` and that feature's own switch decide.
config.aiProviders.item.id: A stable id for this endpoint: letters, digits, `_` and `-` only, because the id is part of the key its API key is stored under.
config.aiProviders.item.name: The display name. It is what the consent question, the log and the settings page call this endpoint, so it should identify the machine or service the content goes to.
config.aiProviders.item.baseUrl: The endpoint base URL, used exactly as written apart from a trailing slash. It must be `http:` or `https:` and must not carry credentials; the service's API path (`/v1`, or Azure's own path) has to be part of it, because nothing is appended but `/chat/completions` and `/models`.
config.aiProviders.item.auth: How a request authenticates: `bearer` sends `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, `api-key-header` sends `api-key: <key>` (Azure's spelling), and `none` sends no credential at all (common for a server on this machine). The key itself is stored in the editor's secret storage, never here.
config.aiProviders.item.models: The models this endpoint offers, as `{ id, name }`. This is a declaration rather than a whitelist: it fills in the model chooser and it is what `forgejoToolkit.aiModelBindings` can name, while a model id typed by hand is still accepted. An empty list is not a failure.
config.aiProviders.item.headers: Extra header names this endpoint needs, such as `api-version` (sent as a query parameter rather than as a header). Only the **names** live here; each value is stored in the editor's secret storage under `forgejoToolkit.aiProviderHeader.<id>.<headerName>`. A name that collides with the `auth` style (`Authorization` / `api-key`) is reported and the `auth` style wins.
config.aiTransport.title: AI: Model Transport
config.aiTransport.description: Which transport an AI feature asks for a model when the feature has no entry in `forgejoToolkit.aiModelBindings` (that entry is an override, and it always wins). `auto` prefers the chat models this editor offers and only considers the configured default endpoint — `forgejoToolkit.aiDefaultProvider` and `forgejoToolkit.aiDefaultModel` — when the editor offers none; `vscode-lm` always uses the editor's models; `openai-compatible` always uses the configured default endpoint. There is no switching between the two: a transport that fails reports the failure rather than quietly asking the other one. The whole area is closed while `forgejoToolkit.aiEnabled` is off, whichever value this holds.
config.aiTransport.enumDescriptions.auto: Prefer the chat models this editor offers; use the configured default endpoint only when the editor offers no model.
config.aiTransport.enumDescriptions.vsco: Always use the chat models this editor offers. With no model available the feature reports that and stops; it never falls back to a configured endpoint.
config.aiTransport.enumDescriptions.open: Always use the configured default endpoint. With no usable endpoint, key or default the feature reports why and stops; it never falls back to this editor's models.
config.aiDefaultProvider.title: AI: Default Endpoint
config.aiDefaultProvider.description: The `id` of the endpoint in `forgejoToolkit.aiProviders` that a direct request goes to when the feature has no entry of its own in `forgejoToolkit.aiModelBindings`. Setting this and `forgejoToolkit.aiDefaultModel` is what makes `openai-compatible` — and the endpoint half of `auto` — usable without binding each feature one by one; an entry in `forgejoToolkit.aiModelBindings` for a feature still overrides this default for that feature. A default that names an endpoint which is not configured fails and names it rather than choosing another endpoint. Both this and `forgejoToolkit.aiDefaultModel` have to be set: one without the other is not a destination, and no model is guessed for an endpoint.
config.aiDefaultModel.title: AI: Default Model
config.aiDefaultModel.description: The model name the default endpoint is asked for, exactly as that endpoint expects it. It is free text: the endpoint's `models` list is a declaration, not a whitelist. Only used together with `forgejoToolkit.aiDefaultProvider`.
config.aiModelBindings.title: AI: Per-Feature Model Overrides
config.aiModelBindings.description: Which endpoint and model **one** AI feature uses, as a list of `{ feature, providerId, modelId }`. This is an override on top of the default: a feature with no entry here follows `forgejoToolkit.aiDefaultProvider` / `forgejoToolkit.aiDefaultModel` (or, with no default configured, the rules of `forgejoToolkit.aiTransport` as they were before the default existed), and the entry is how one feature may be given a stronger or more private model of its own. An override is the most specific statement there is: it names the destination, so it is used whatever `forgejoToolkit.aiTransport` says and whatever the default says, and an entry that names an endpoint which is not configured, or one that cannot be used, fails and names the entry rather than quietly choosing another endpoint. `providerId` must match an `id` in `forgejoToolkit.aiProviders`, and `modelId` is free text — the endpoint's model name, which does not have to appear in that endpoint's `models` list. An entry naming a feature this build does not know is ignored.
config.aiModelBindings.item.feature: The AI feature this binding is for.
config.aiModelBindings.item.providerId: The `id` of an entry in `forgejoToolkit.aiProviders`. An id that matches nothing fails the run by name instead of resolving to another endpoint.
config.aiModelBindings.item.modelId: The model name to ask for, exactly as the endpoint expects it. It is free text: the endpoint's `models` list is a declaration, not a whitelist.
config.aiModelRequestTimeoutMs.title: AI: Endpoint Idle Timeout (ms)
config.aiModelRequestTimeoutMs.descripti: How long an endpoint may send **nothing** before a request to it is aborted (default 30000). This is an idle window, not a total limit: a model answer may legitimately take minutes, so a stream that keeps arriving survives however long it takes, and only a silent endpoint is stopped. A second, wider limit applies to the request as a whole — ten times this value — so a stream that dribbles forever cannot hold the window open. Both numbers are written to the debug log, and a value outside 1000–600000 reads as the default.
config.worktreeOpenMode.enumDescriptions: Ask each time how to open a worktree
Open worktrees in a new VS Code window
Open worktrees in the current VS Code window

capabilities.untrustedWorkspaces.descrip: Forgejo Toolkit reads and caches repository state (git worktrees, the extension's cache directory and instance configuration), so it is disabled in Restricted Mode until you trust the workspace.
